messages.subject: Latexdiff
parts:
I meant to send this message to the dev list.




Daniel



---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu>
Date: Sat, Sep 29, 2012 at 9:38 PM
Subject: Latexdiff
To: stan-...@googlegroups.com


Ben,

That looks awesome and useful. Would you mind helping us set it up? I
can automate it once we have clear instructions on how to build using
a tool like that.

I'm a little swamped now with the vectorization to pull it off anytime soon.

Daniel

On Sep 29, 2012 9:00 PM, "Ben Goodrich" <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Daniel or Bob,
>
> I think we should also compile a version of the manual that highlights the changes relative to the previous version of the manual so that people can quickly find where user-relevant changes are discussed. Maybe something like
>
> https://eothred.wordpress.com/2010/11/07/latexdiff-and-git/
>
> Ben
>
> On Saturday, September 29, 2012 8:48:13 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
>>
>> Bob has written it into the latest version of the manual. Section 5 starting on page 29.
>>
>> For anyone that hasn't downloaded the latest versions of the manual or the software, please do. There have been many improvements to both.
>>
>> Daniel
>>
>> On Sep 29, 2012 8:37 PM, "Andrew Gelman" <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>
>>> We should definitely have an example in the manual using the print statement to debug (if we don't have that already in the manual).
>>> A
>>>
>>> On Sep 29, 2012, at 8:33 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>>>
>>> Hi Terrance,
>>>
>>> For help debugging models --- particularly for models as complicated as this --- it would help if you could narrow the problem down yourself as much as possible before posting. Here is what I did to figure it out. If you haven't already done so, definitely install version 1.0.2 because it introduces the print() function.
>>>
>>> I added these print lines to your .stan file:
>>> /* Formulate c1[i,d] and c2[i,d], mean of latent response or multi-variate trait in ordered_logistic model */
>>> print("Delta= ", Delta[teacher1[1]][1,1]);
>>> print("Phi= ", Phi[section1[1]][1,1]);
>>> print("Theta= ", Theta[session1[1]][1,1]);
>>> print("Zeta= ", Zeta[session_rater1[1]][1,1]);
>>> print("Beta_mean= ", Beta_mean[rater1[1]][1,1]);
>>> for( i in 1:N1 ) for( d in 1:D ) c1[i,d] <- Delta[teacher1[i]][d,1] + Phi[section1[i]][d,1] + Theta[session1[i]][d,1] + Zeta[session_rater1[i]][d,1] + Beta_mean[rater1[i]][d,1];
>>> for( i in 1:N2 ) for( d in 1:D ) c2[i,d] <- Delta[teacher2[i]][d,2] + Phi[section2[i]][d,2] + Theta[session2[i]][d,2] + Zeta[session_rater2[i]][d,2] + Beta_mean[rater2[i]][d,2];
>>>
>>>
>>> I then compiled compiled with -g (you may have to add that in the Makefile) and O=0 and ran it under gdb
>>>
>>> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp/Terrance$ gdb --args ./modelFAcum_lkj --data=datstan.Rdump
>>> GNU gdb (GDB) 7.4.1-debian
>>> Copyright (C) 2012 Free Software Foundation, Inc.
>>> License GPLv3+: GNU GPL version 3 or later <http://gnu.org/licenses/gpl.html>
>>> This is free software: you are free to change and redistribute it.
>>> There is NO WARRANTY, to the extent permitted by law. Type "show copying"
>>> and "show warranty" for details.
>>> This GDB was configured as "x86_64-linux-gnu".
>>> For bug reporting instructions, please see:
>>> <http://www.gnu.org/software/gdb/bugs/>...
>>> Reading symbols from /tmp/Terrance/modelFAcum_lkj...done.
>>> (gdb) catch throw
>>> Catchpoint 1 (throw)
>>> (gdb) run
>>> Starting program: /tmp/Terrance/modelFAcum_lkj --data=datstan.Rdump
>>> [Thread debugging using libthread_db enabled]
>>> Using host libthread_db library "/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libthread_db.so.1".
>>> Delta= 1.04147
>>> Phi= -1.2006
>>> Theta= 1.17
>>> Zeta= 1.49939
>>> Beta_mean= nan
>>> Catchpoint 1 (exception thrown), 0x00007ffff791db90 in __cxa_throw () from /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libstdc++.so.6
>>>
>>>
>>> At this point, you could fool around in gdb to investigate further; Google shows lots of HOWTOs for gdb.
>>>
>>> But the print() statements in the .stan file indicate that the elements of c1 (and c2) are nan because the elements of Beta_mean are nan, which happens because you attempted to use it before filling it:
>>>
>>> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp/Terrance$ grep -n Beta_mean modelFAcum_lkj.stan
>>> 79: matrix[D,M] Beta_mean[Rr];
>>> 97: print("Beta_mean= ", Beta_mean[rater1[1]][1,1]);
>>> 98: for( i in 1:N1 ) for( d in 1:D ) c1[i,d] <- Delta[teacher1[i]][d,1] + Phi[section1[i]][d,1] + Theta[session1[i]][d,1] + Zeta[session_rater1[i]][d,1] + Beta_mean[rater1[i]][d,1];
>>> 99: for( i in 1:N2 ) for( d in 1:D ) c2[i,d] <- Delta[teacher2[i]][d,2] + Phi[section2[i]][d,2] + Theta[session2[i]][d,2] + Zeta[session_rater2[i]][d,2] + Beta_mean[rater2[i]][d,2];
>>> 118: for( r in 1:Rr ) Beta_mean[r] <- Beta[r] + mean_Beta;
>>> 228: /* functions of multivariate hierarchical parameters, Delta, Phi, Theta, Zeta, Beta_mean */
>>>
>>>
>>> So, I think line 118 (maybe 113 in your original .stan file) needs to be moved farther up or something.
>>>
>>> Ben
>>>
>>> On Saturday, September 29, 2012 7:30:23 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
>>>>
>>>> I have 2 sets of multivariate ordinal responses, y1[i,d] and y2[i,d], modeled as ordered_logistic with intrinsic traits, c1[i,d] and c2[i,d] for d = 1, ..., D. The intrinsic traits are connected by sharing hierarchical multivariate random effects. For example, there is D x M, Delta[T], and Phi[S] where d = 1, ... D are multivariate dimension and m = 1, ..., (M=2) are alternate measurement modes. Then c1[i,d] = Delta[teacher1[i]][d,1] + Phi[section1[i]][d,1] and c2[i,d] = Delta[teacher2[i]][d,2] + Phi[section2[i]][d,2]. Each latent response has ordered cutpoints, D x ncut, lim1 and lim2.
>>>>
>>>> The model crashes during sampling, with the following error message:
>>>>
>>>> SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'modelFAcum_lkj' NOW (CHAIN 1).
>>>> Error in sampler$call_sampler(args_list[[i]]) :
>>>> Error in function stan::prob::ordered_logistic(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is 1.#QNAN:0, but must be finite!
>>>>
>>>> This indicates to me that one or more of the ordered cutpoint values spins off to infinity. In the attached model, the cutpoints are defined such that the first is fixed to 0 as a hard constraint, which is necessary to establish location identifiability. (A soft constraint of an informative prior isn't sufficient). That said, I ran a simpler version, taking away this constraint to see if the problem went away, but it didn't - I received the exact same error message.
>>>>
>>>> The model section includes statement blocks for each of the hierarchical multivariate random effects. lp__ is incremented using a matrix normal distribution, which is the equivalent of vectorizing the parameters and using a structured kronecker product of D x D and M x M covariance matrices. The first set of random effect parameters, Delta, composes the D x D covariance under a factor analytic structure, where cov(Delta) = Lambda * Lambda' + Theta, for D x K, Lambda where K < D. A lower triangular structure is enforced for Lambda (for rotation identification) by reading a binary "pick" matrix, B, filled with 0's and 1's that multiplies against a D x K matrix of parameters, Lambda_s, with each element sampled from a standard normal.
>>>>
>>>> My intuition is that placing informative priors on the cutpoints won't fix the problem, but maybe all parameters need relatively informative priors due to the model complexity to accomplish joint sampling. I let Stan generate initial parameter values, which should be fine (under the declared constraints). That said, I'm now experimenting with inputing my own initial values.
>>>>
>>>> This model is a first step to see if i'm able to get Stan to work. I'm intending to replace the ordered_logistic construction with a latent response. I've created another script that employs tricks generously offered from Stan developers to get around the lack of functionality for by-element truncation points. Such a construction will eventually allow me to generalize the logit link function to something semi-parametric (e.g. multimodal). I have successfully implemented similar models in JAGS, but for M = 1 mode. That said, I have combined datasets in JAGS under this type of model that share portions of multivariate random effect parameters in a similar fashion. Because JAGS requires conjugacy for covariance matrices (and doesn't allow direct updates to the joint log probability) I would have to define D*M x D*M unstructured covariance matrices to use JAGS.
>>>>
>>>> Thanks for your time and help. Terrance
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> --
>>>> Thank you, Terrance Savitsky
>>>
>>>

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Latexdiff
parts:
Perhaps the most promising git-centric wrapper around latexdiff seems to be

https://gitorious.org/git-latexdiff

However, latexdiff was not particularly close to generating a useful (and syntactically correct) .tex file with the differences in the manual for v1.0.2 relative to v1.0.1 . I started to manually fix the latex errors but gave up after fixing about half of them. In particular, it has problems with \Verb and some with displaymath.

This might get easier in the future when there are a smaller number of changes to the manual, but it looks like it will never be fully automatic.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Latexdiff
parts:
On Sunday, September 30, 2012 1:22:18 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
Perhaps the most promising git-centric wrapper around latexdiff seems to be

https://gitorious.org/git-latexdiff

However, latexdiff was not particularly close to generating a useful (and syntactically correct) .tex file with the differences in the manual for v1.0.2 relative to v1.0.1 . I started to manually fix the latex errors but gave up after fixing about half of them. In particular, it has problems with \Verb and some with displaymath.

This might get easier in the future when there are a smaller number of changes to the manual, but it looks like it will never be fully automatic.

Ben

OK, I will probably regret saying this, but we could (in principle) write our own script to use instead of latexdiff (which was written well before git existed).

First, the on-screen output of

git diff --unified=0 --inter-hunk-context=0 --word-diff --color=always v1.0.1 v1.0.2 src/docs/stan-reference/

is pretty useful and is probably adequate for people to skim as long as they can compile latex in their head. The arguments

--unified=0 prints 0 lines of context
--inter-hunk-context=0 similar to --unified=0
--word-diff looks for changes by "word" (which basically means delimited by whitespace)
--color=always makes additions show up in green and deletions in red
v1.0.1 v1.0.2 means between these two tags
src/docs/stan-reference/ means everything in that directory

In practice, the unwritten script would probably process one .tex file at a time.

I am attaching the output of the above as all_changes.txt in case you don't have git readily available. You loose the coloration but you can still see additions, which are enclosed by {+ and +} and deletions, which are enclosed by [- and -].

What we want to do is temporarily add markers to the .tex files so that they will indicate what has been added (and possibly deleted) and then compile a temporary version of the manual that has the changes highlighted. This is pretty straightforward for the case where whole lines have been added since v1.0.1 . Using the example of acknowledgements.tex, this opqaque command

git diff --unified=0 --inter-hunk-context=0 --word-diff --color=never v1.0.1 v1.0.2 src/docs/stan-reference/acknowledgements.tex | grep ^\{+.*+}$ | sed 's/{+%+}//' | sed '/\\.*{.*}.*+}$/ d' | sed 's/^{+/s\//' | sed 's/+}$/\/\\\\A{\&}\//' > /tmp/sedscript.sh

yields a sedscript.sh file with these lines

s/Thanks to Jeffrey Arnold for submitting code patches and reporting/\\A{&}/
s/a whole bunch of bugs for earlier versions. /\\A{&}/
s/Thanks to Jeffrey Arnold, Eric N.~Brown, and Wayne Folta for/\\A{&}/
s/submitting documentation patches./\\A{&}/
s/We're really thankful to everyone who's had the patience to try/\\A{&}/
s/to get Stan working and reported bugs.  All the gory details are/\\A{&}/
s/available from Stan's issue tracker at the following URL./\\A{&}/

where the & basically means "substitute the thing between the preceding / / here". Then

sed -i -f /tmp/sedscript.sh src/docs/stan-reference/acknowledgements.tex

changes the existing acknowledgements.tex file so it now has lines like

\subsection*{Code  and Doc Patches}

\A{Thanks to Jeffrey Arnold for submitting code patches and reporting}
\A{a whole bunch of bugs for earlier versions. }

\A{Thanks to Jeffrey Arnold, Eric N.~Brown, and Wayne Folta for}
\A{submitting documentation patches.}

\subsection*{Bug Reports}

\A{We're really thankful to everyone who's had the patience to try}
\A{to get Stan working and reported bugs.  All the gory details are}
\A{available from Stan's issue tracker at the following URL.}

Thus, if we define the \A{} macro with a \newcommand to be green text or underlined or something and compile, then the parts in the acknowledgments section added before v1.0.2 was tagged would be highlighted accordingly in the PDF.

And then we do

git reset --hard HEAD

and it's as if nothing ever happened to acknowledgements.tex in master.

Maybe that is already enough, but we could also handle intra-line edits in a roughly similar fashion. So, the question becomes is it worth making such a script and robustifying it?

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Latexdiff
parts:
On Monday, October 1, 2012 2:17:13 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
OK, I will probably regret saying this, but we could (in principle) write our own script to use instead of latexdiff (which was written well before git existed).

Doing this is somewhat annoying, but it is manageable. This script I wrote

#!/bin/bash -e

OLD_VERSION=$1
NEW_VERSION=$2

ADDED_LINE=^\{+.*+}$
IGNORE_COMMENT_LINE='/{+%\s*+}/d'
IGNORE_LINE_WITH_LEADING_SLASH='/^{+\\/d'
IGNORE_LATEX_MACROS='/\\[A-Za-z]*{.*}/d'
IGNORE_ALL_BRACES='/^{+.*[{}].*+}$/d'
FIX_COMMENTS='s@%@}@'
ESCAPE_SLASH='s@\\@\\\\@'
ESCAPE_AMPERSAND='s@\&@\\\&@'
ESCAPE_AT='s@\@@\\\@@'
ESCAPE_BRACKET='s@\[@\\\[@'
DELETE_BRACEPLUS='s@^{+@s\@\^@'
ADD_MACRO='s@+}$@\$\@\\\\A{\&}\@@'

TEX_FILES=`ls *.tex`
for TEX_FILE in $TEX_FILES; do
        if [ "stan-reference.tex" = "$TEX_FILE" ]; then
                continue
        fi
        git diff --unified=0 --inter-hunk-context=0 --word-diff --color=never $OLD_VERSION $NEW_VERSION $TEX_FILE | \
        grep ${ADDED_LINE} | \
        sed ${IGNORE_LINE_WITH_LEADING_SLASH} | \
        sed ${IGNORE_COMMENT_LINE} | \
#       sed ${IGNORE_LATEX_MACROS} | \
        sed ${IGNORE_ALL_BRACES} | \
        sed ${FIX_COMMENTS} | \
        sed ${ESCAPE_SLASH} | \
        sed ${ESCAPE_AMPERSAND} | \
        sed ${ESCAPE_AT} | \
        sed ${ESCAPE_BRACKET} | \
        sed ${DELETE_BRACEPLUS} | \
        sed ${ADD_MACRO} > \
        sedscript.sh
        echo 'Processing ' $TEX_FILE
        sed -i -f sedscript.sh $TEX_FILE
        rm sedscript.sh
done


essentially puts (most) lines that were added between v1.0.1 and v1.0.2 within a \A{} macro and I have for now done \newcommand{\A}{\textcolor{green}} although we could do something else to be better for colorblind people. The attached PDF manual has this done for the Appendices only (starting at p.183).

The main annoying thing is our frequent use of the Verbatim environment. Thus, something like

\begin{Verbatim}
model {
  \A{real x;}
}
\end{Verbatim}

comes out literally instead of just putting real x; in green. We can get around this by using the alltt package / environment in these situations, which is like Verbatim in terms of spacing but processes interior macros. The annoying thing with that is that you have to escape the braces to get them to compile as braces, so this works:

\begin{alltt}
model \{
  \A{real x;}
\}
\end{alltt}

I didn't go though and escape every brace in the Appendices though, so some things are a little off. Also, it is a bit hit-and-miss with what it currently makes green because I was conservative in only processing lines that would (probably) not break the compilation (too badly). But that could probably be improved as well as processing in-line edits in addition to entirely new lines.

So, my question basically is do people have opinions as to whether this is worth regularly doing for the whole reference manual?

Ben
